topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: A report sorts jobs by priority, but equal-priority jobs change relative order. Another routine calls binary search on unsorted data and treats an arbitrary result as a valid answer. Standard algorithms remove repetitive loops only when their preconditions and result semantics are understood.

blocks.text: A standard algorithm is a named agreement between the caller and the library. The caller supplies a valid range, an appropriate operation, and any required ordering or destination storage. The library supplies the behavior described by that algorithm. Neither side can quietly omit its responsibilities. A beautifully named call with an invalid comparator is less reliable than a simple loop whose invariant is correct.

blocks.text: For HarborWorks, the important question is not whether a hand-written loop can be replaced. It is whether the replacement makes the report’s meaning easier to inspect. “Keep the original arrival order within each priority” is a stability requirement. “Produce exactly one converted value for every accepted sample” is an output-extent requirement. “Reject a total that cannot be represented” is a numeric requirement. State those requirements before choosing algorithms.

topics.title: 17.1 Searching and Sorting Collections
topics.summary: Searching and sorting algorithms answer different questions over ranges with different requirements. Linear search needs an equality or predicate relationship. Binary-search operations need the relevant partitioning or ordering precondition. Sorting requires a valid ordering relation and suitable iterator capabilities.

blocks.text: A search result represents a position under a particular question. Equality search asks whether an element compares equal to the requested value. Predicate search asks whether an element satisfies a condition. A boundary search asks where a partition changes. These questions can yield the same iterator on one example and different iterators on the next. Tests should make the distinction visible rather than relying on a conveniently chosen input.

blocks.text: Consider the ordered sequence 10, 20, 20, 40. The lower bound for 20 identifies the first 20, while the upper bound identifies 40. Together those positions delimit the equal values. The lower bound for 30 also identifies 40, but that does not mean 30 exists. The lower bound for 50 is end, which cannot be dereferenced. An empty sequence produces end immediately. Work through these cases on paper before writing the membership check.

blocks.text: For a sorted range, use the same meaningful comparison policy when sorting and searching. Sorting names without regard to case and then searching under ordinary byte ordering does not preserve the assumed arrangement. A comparator’s consistency is part of the stored representation. The issue is not fixed by testing one spelling that happens to occupy the same position under both orderings.

blocks.text: The common description of binary search as logarithmic also needs context. Comparison count and iterator movement are different costs. A lower-bound operation over forward iterators can require linear iterator increments even while using logarithmically many comparisons. An ordered associative container’s member lookup can exploit its own structure directly. Avoid replacing a container’s suitable member search with a generic iterator algorithm merely because both have similar names.

blocks.text: Use a returned iterator only while the searched range remains valid. A successful search does not give the element an independent lifetime. If the owner changes, reallocates, or disappears, the search result may no longer identify a usable element. For an API that needs to retain identity across changes, return a stable identifier or an owning result under a documented contract rather than casually retaining an iterator.

topics.summary: std::stable_sort preserves the original relative order of elements equivalent under the comparator. Sorting jobs only by priority therefore retains their arrival sequence within each priority group. Ordinary std::sort does not promise that stability.

blocks.text: A comparator must express a strict weak ordering for these algorithms. Returning true for equal elements through <= violates that contract. Avoid comparators whose answer changes during sorting because of mutable external state. When deterministic tie-breaking is required rather than original-order stability, compare a tuple of explicit keys such as priority and identifier.

violates that contract. Avoid comparators whose answer changes during sorting because of mutable external state. When deterministic tie-breaking is required rather than original-order stability, compare a tuple of explicit keys such as priority and identifier.

blocks.text: Strict weak ordering is a semantic requirement, not a compiler switch. The comparison must not say that an element precedes itself. It must behave consistently across repeated comparisons, and its ordering and equivalence relationships must satisfy the required laws. A comparator returning left.priority <= right.priority is not “more inclusive”; it gives the wrong answer when priorities are equal.

is not “more inclusive”; it gives the wrong answer when priorities are equal.

blocks.text: A practical review starts with three records. Ask whether comparing a record with itself returns false. Ask whether both directions can return true. Then test a chain of records and the equivalence groups induced by the comparison. These small tests do not prove every comparator correct, but they expose several common mistakes. A comparator with complex external state deserves a simpler redesign before it deserves a larger test suite.

blocks.text: Floating-point keys require deliberate handling of exceptional values. Ordinary less-than over a domain containing NaNs does not automatically provide a suitable ordering for every sorting use. Do not assume that a successful compilation or a familiar operator proves the semantic requirement. Restrict the input domain to finite values or define and test a policy for exceptional values before sorting such data.

blocks.text: Stability and determinism are related but distinct. Stable sorting preserves the prior order within comparator-equivalent groups. If input order itself changes between runs, the final order can change while remaining perfectly stable. A report that must be independent of arrival order needs an explicit secondary key, such as a unique ID. Sorting by (priority, id) expresses that contract directly; stable sorting by priority expresses a different contract.

blocks.text: Also decide whether sorting is permitted to mutate the accepted dataset. The report examples often sort an owning snapshot so the stored source remains in ingestion order. Sorting in place may be more economical, but it changes the owner’s observable sequence. This is a design choice, not a harmless implementation detail when other operations depend on arrival order or positions.

blocks.text: Passing destination.begin() for an empty vector would not create elements merely because the algorithm writes through it. Either size the destination first or use an insertion adapter. The sample values are bounded so squaring is representable. A general numeric transformation needs its own overflow, precision, and domain policy.

blocks.text: An output iterator grants a way to write; it does not necessarily grant room to write. begin() on an empty vector is not an append operation. Reserving capacity does not create elements either. A transformation into existing positions requires a destination with enough constructed elements. An insertion adapter grows a compatible container through its insertion interface. Choose one model and make its preconditions obvious.

blocks.text: A useful trace records input extent, output extent, and destination capacity separately. Suppose five input records produce five strings. A pre-sized vector of five strings supplies five writable objects. An empty vector with capacity five supplies storage but no string elements at those positions. A back-insertion adapter constructs elements as it appends them. Those three states can have similar memory allocations while permitting different operations.

blocks.text: A one-input transform can perform an in-place operation when the documented overlap rules are satisfied, such as replacing each integer with its own square. That does not authorize arbitrary overlapping input and output ranges. When unsure, choose a separate destination and inspect the algorithm’s exact contract. An optimization that relies on a prohibited overlap is not an optimization of the same program.

blocks.text: Failure behavior also depends on the destination strategy. A transform that appends directly to a public vector can leave a prefix appended when the conversion throws. A transform into a private candidate can discard that candidate while leaving the accepted public value unchanged. RAII cleans up constructed strings in either case, but only the second arrangement supplies the stronger public-state guarantee. Cleanup and rollback remain different properties.

topics.title: Review and solution reasoning
topics.summary: An algorithm name communicates useful intent only together with its requirements. Stable order does not imply arrival-independent order. A boundary does not imply membership. Reserved storage does not imply writable elements. A wide final variable does not repair narrow intermediate arithmetic. The strongest solution makes these distinctions part of the interface and tests, rather than leaving them as comments beside a fragile call.
